title: H-Index
statement: Given an array citations where citations[i] is the number of citations received by the researcher's i-th paper, return their h-index. The h-index is the largest value h such that the researcher has published at least h papers that have each been cited at least h times. The remaining papers may have any number of citations, including zero. Note that h is bounded by the number of papers as well as by their citation counts.
realWorld: The metric itself decides academic hiring and grant review, but the shape is general: 'the largest threshold t such that at least t items clear t' is how you size a cache tier from an access histogram ('how many keys are hit at least that many times?'), pick a rate-limit bucket, or choose a self-consistent percentile cut. It is the same self-referential threshold every time — the answer appears on both sides of the condition.

examples.explanation: Sorted ascending: [0,1,3,5,6]. Three papers (3, 5 and 6) have at least 3 citations each, so h = 3 holds. h = 4 would need four papers with at least 4 citations and only two papers clear 4.

Sorted ascending: [1,1,3]. All three papers have at least 1 citation, so h = 1 holds. h = 2 needs two papers with at least 2 citations each and only the paper with 3 clears 2. Reading h as 'the number of papers with a nonzero count' gives 3 and is wrong.

One paper, cited 100 times. h = 1 holds; h = 2 is impossible because there is only one paper. This is the case that shows h is capped by the paper count, not by the citation counts — misreading the definition as 'the largest citation count' gives 100.

constraints: the answer is always between 0 and n inclusive

bruteForce.idea: Try every candidate value of h from n downwards, and for each one count how many papers clear that bar. Return the first candidate whose count reaches it.
code: for (int citation : citations) {   // a fresh count of every paper, for every candidate h
bruteForce.whySlow: There are n+1 candidate values of h and each one rescans all n papers to ask 'how many clear this bar?'. Those counts are not independent: as h drops by one, the set of qualifying papers can only grow, and it grows by exactly the papers whose citation count equals the new h. Every scan therefore recounts every paper that every previous scan already counted — it is a running total being recomputed from scratch n times instead of being carried. With n = 5000 that is 25 million comparisons to produce 5001 numbers that differ from their neighbours by a handful of papers each.

patternIdentification: The condition couples a rank with a value: the h-th largest element must itself be at least h. Whenever the answer is phrased in terms of 'the k-th largest' or 'how many items clear a threshold', put the data in order first — once sorted, an element's rank is its position, so the two quantities being compared sit in the same place and one scan settles all of them. The second half transfers just as widely: when the values are bounded by something small, counting sort replaces the comparison sort and the whole thing becomes linear. Here the bound is free, because h can never exceed n, so any citation count above n is indistinguishable from n and can be clamped to it.

optimized.idea: Sort ascending, then scan from the low end. After sorting, the paper at index i has exactly n - i papers at or above it in the order, all with at least citations[i] citations. So if citations[i] >= n - i, then n - i papers each have at least n - i citations and n - i is a valid h. Scanning i upwards, n - i shrinks, so the first index that satisfies the test yields the largest valid h. The linear variant drops the comparison sort: clamp each count to n, tally the counts into a histogram, then sweep h downwards accumulating 'papers with at least h citations' and stop when that running total reaches h.
code: int papers = n - i;   // papers from index i to the end all have >= citations[i]
// O(n) variant: h can never exceed n, so clamp every count to n and counting-sort.
int[] papersWith = new int[n + 1];   // n + 1, because h = n is a legal answer

complexity.time: O(n log n) sorted, O(n) counting

commonMistakes: Misreading the definition as 'the largest citation count' or 'the number of papers with at least one citation'. [100] then returns 100 or 1 depending on which misreading you chose, and [1,3,1] returns 3 — the definition, not the algorithm, is the actual failure mode of this problem.

Returning the index i rather than the count n - i. On [0,1,3,5,6] the loop stops at i = 2 and returns 2 instead of 3; the two numbers are close enough that the output still looks like a plausible h-index, so the bug survives eyeballing.

Sizing the counting array as new int[n] instead of new int[n + 1]. h = n is a legal answer — five papers with five citations each gives h = 5 — so the downward sweep's very first read at index n throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, and only on the inputs where every citation count is high.
